title: The dark house
hookLine: a blind servant, Harpaste, insists the house is dark; we blame everything but ourselves (Letters 50)

lines: A WOMAN WHO DIDN'T KNOW SHE WAS BLIND.
cards: The traffic made me late. The weather put me in a mood. My coworker made me snap.

Count the sentences in a single day that put the cause of trouble somewhere outside the skin. In the fiftieth letter, Seneca tells a story about this, about a woman in his household who lost her sight and didn't know it.
He admits it sounds hard to believe. He tells it to make a point about himself and his readers, not about her.

teach.h: HARPASTE SAYS THE HOUSE IS DARK.
teach.b: Harpaste had belonged to his wife's household, kept to amuse, a custom Seneca says he himself disliked, and she stayed on in his house as an inherited charge. She had suddenly gone blind, but she didn't know it.
She kept asking her attendant to take her somewhere else, because, she said, the house was dark. What we laugh at in her, Seneca writes, happens to all of us.
Nobody thinks they're greedy. Nobody admits they're stingy. The ambitious person says it's just how you get on in Rome.
The extravagant one says the city demands it. It's my youth, says another. It's not my fault, I can't help it.
Our trouble isn't outside us, he says. It's inside, settled deep in our vital organs, and because we don't know we're sick, getting well is harder. Then the hope.

It's never too late to be healed, and the mind, unlike the body, can be reshaped at any age, if we start by admitting where the dark actually is. That admission isn't self-hatred. It's the first piece of good news.
If the dark is in the house, you have to move. If it's in me, I can do something about it, wherever I am.

how: Stoic practitioners often review the day by asking, of each frustration, which part came from outside and which part came from their own judgment or habit.

o: a servant who ran away from Seneca's household
a Roman goddess of the night and its shadows
the woman who went blind and said the house was dark

games.q: the dark house — tap the pairs.
p: the mind can heal at any age

s: Seneca tells the story to mock Harpaste
he says what we laugh at in her happens to all of us.
Seneca says our trouble is settled inside us, not outside
and because we don't know we're sick, healing is harder.
Seneca thinks it's too late for adults to change
he says it's never too late to be healed.

games.q: you snapped at someone and your first thought is 'the day made me do it.' what does Harpaste's story suggest?
o: look for the part of the dark that's in you.
insist harder that the day was bad.
games.why: Harpaste blamed the house; Seneca says we all do the same, and healing starts with seeing where the dark really is.

practice: Think back to one moment this week you blamed on circumstance, the traffic, the weather, someone else's mood, and replay it gently. Then try the other sentence, just to see how it fits: part of that was in me.
No scolding; just turning on a light in the right room.

wordCard.voice: Harpaste. Seneca's story of the woman who went blind and blamed the house for the dark, when the darkness was in her own eyes. Today's word.
